finance32
financeevery job7

The rows come sorted by their first column, as the Example database sorts them, which puts "every team" between "data" and "finance". At work rows come in no fixed order: sort them with ORDER_BY, or in pandas.

Keep only the subtotals

is_total in HAVING keeps or leaves out subtotal rows, since HAVING tests the rows GROUP_BY made, subtotals included. Here only each team's total and the grand total. The column it tests, job_events.job_id, must be in SELECT too: without it, a subtotal row looks like the rows it totals, so the Toolbox refuses it.

team_totals = statement(  # -> Statement
    SELECT(job_owners.team, job_events.job_id,
           AS(count_rows(where=equals(job_events.event_type, "start")), "runs")),
    FROM(job_events),
    owner_on_day(job_events.job_id, job_events.dt, first_day="2026-09-18",
                 last_day="2026-09-24"),
    WHERE(between(job_events.dt, "2026-09-18", "2026-09-24")),
    GROUP_BY(rollup(job_owners.team, job_events.job_id)),
    HAVING(is_total(job_events.job_id)),
)
run_query(team_totals, query)  # -> DataFrame

Result, computed in pandas, not by running this Hive

teamjob_idruns
NULLNULL14
dataNULL7
financeNULL7
Other sets of subtotals

rollup drops its columns from the right, first the job, then the team: each team over its jobs, never each job over its teams. For every mix, use cube(job_owners.team, job_owners.owner): each team over every owner, each owner over every team, and the grand total. To pick the sets yourself, list them with grouping_sets([job_owners.team], [job_owners.owner], []). A plain column beside a rollup is in every set, so GROUP_BY(job_events.dt, rollup(job_owners.team)) totals each day's teams, and never adds days together.

Check it worked

Each week's runs are its days' runs added up, and the weeks' runs add up to the 28 runs over the 14 days. Check both from a count per day, which the Example database runs, with each day's Monday worked out in pandas: days.dt.weekday is 0 on a Monday and 6 on a Sunday, so taking that many days off a day gives its Monday.

import pandas as pd
starts_per_day = statement(  # -> Statement
    SELECT(job_events.dt, AS(count_rows(), "starts")),
    FROM(job_events),
    WHERE(equals(job_events.event_type, "start"),
          between(job_events.dt, "2026-09-11", "2026-09-24")),
    GROUP_BY(job_events.dt),
)
per_day = run_query(starts_per_day, query)  # -> DataFrame
days = pd.to_datetime(per_day["dt"])
per_day["week"] = (days - pd.to_timedelta(days.dt.weekday, unit="D")).dt.strftime(
    "%Y-%m-%d")
per_day.groupby("week")["starts"].sum()

2026-09-21     9

These are starts_per_week's rows added up per week: 3 + 1 + 1, 7 + 5 + 2 and 4 + 4 + 1.

And each team's subtotal is its jobs' runs added up. A plain GROUP_BY, which the Example database runs, counts the same:

runs_per_team = statement(  # -> Statement
    SELECT(job_owners.team,
           AS(count_rows(where=equals(job_events.event_type, "start")), "runs")),
    FROM(job_events),
    owner_on_day(job_events.job_id, job_events.dt, first_day="2026-09-18",
                 last_day="2026-09-24"),
    WHERE(between(job_events.dt, "2026-09-18", "2026-09-24")),
    GROUP_BY(job_owners.team),
)
run_query(runs_per_team, query)  # -> DataFrame

7 and 7 are the team subtotals above, and they add up to the grand total, 14.

Common mistakes

Adding up each day's count of different jobs

Say a count of the different jobs on each day is already there. Adding up its days looks like the quick way to a week, but a job that ran on five days is in five days' counts, so the week would count it five times. The Toolbox refuses it as you build the Statement:

jobs_per_day = derived("jobs_per_day", statement(  # -> Table
    SELECT(job_events.dt, AS(count_distinct(job_events.job_id), "jobs_that_ran")),
    FROM(job_events),
    WHERE(equals(job_events.event_type, "start"),
          between(job_events.dt, "2026-09-11", "2026-09-24")),
    GROUP_BY(job_events.dt),
))
statement(
    SELECT(AS(week_start(jobs_per_day.dt), "week"),
           AS(sum_of(jobs_per_day.jobs_that_ran), "jobs_that_ran")),
    FROM(jobs_per_day),
    GROUP_BY("week"),
)

Python stops with this message

GuardRefused:
  What happened:  sum_of(jobs_per_day.jobs_that_ran) adds up jobs_per_day.jobs_that_ran, which is a distinct count.
  Why it matters: Averages, ratios and distinct counts don't add up: the average of daily averages is not the weekly average, and a user seen on two days would be counted twice.
  Usual fix:      For a count over the whole span, count again with count_distinct(...) from the rows it was counted from, under your own GROUP_BY: a week's count comes from the week's rows, not from each day's count.
  Opt-out:        sum_of(jobs_per_day.jobs_that_ran, adds_up=True)

Count again from the rows, as jobs_per_week does. A plain count, such as runs, does add up: a week's runs are its days' runs added together. The gallery's re-grouping Worked example shows the wrong number the opt-out gives.

Leaving the week out of GROUP_BY

Without GROUP_BY, the Statement has no groups for the count to count in:

statement(
    SELECT(AS(week_start(job_events.dt), "week"), AS(count_rows(), "starts")),
    FROM(job_events),
    WHERE(equals(job_events.event_type, "start"),
          between(job_events.dt, "2026-09-11", "2026-09-24")),
)

Python stops with this message

GuardRefused:
  What happened:  SELECT has the calculation "week" (from job_events.dt), but the Statement counts or adds up rows and has no GROUP_BY.
  Why it matters: Each output row is one group, so a column that isn't grouped has no single value to show. Hive would refuse the Statement.
  Usual fix:      Add GROUP_BY("week"). A calculation is grouped by the name you gave it with AS.
  Opt-out:        none - this one can't be switched off.

Its fix groups by the name you gave the week, GROUP_BY("week"): one row per week. GROUP_BY(job_events.dt), the column inside week_start, would give one row per day instead.

Reading weeks your days only partly cover

The days you read decide which days each week holds. Counting the days in each week shows it:

days_per_week = statement(  # -> Statement
    SELECT(AS(week_start(job_events.dt), "week"),
           AS(count_distinct(job_events.dt), "days")),
    FROM(job_events),
    WHERE(between(job_events.dt, "2026-09-11", "2026-09-24")),
    GROUP_BY("week"),
)
run_query(days_per_week, query)  # -> DataFrame

Result, computed in pandas, not by running this Hive

weekdays
2026-09-073
2026-09-147
2026-09-214

The first and last weeks hold 3 and 4 days, so their runs look low next to the middle week's, though nothing ran less. To compare weeks, read whole weeks, from a Monday to a Sunday, as week_totals above does; for months, from the 1st to the month's last day.

Adding up a column of subtotals

Each run is counted in its job's row, its team's subtotal and the grand total, so adding up the whole "runs" column in pandas counts every run three times:

int(run_query(runs_per_job, query)["runs"].sum())

Python shows

42

Add up only the rows that aren't subtotals, or read the grand total's own row.

Writing subtotals into a Saved table

A Saved table holds one row for each Key, and subtotal rows repeat the rows they total: a sum over the table would count each row twice. mart.job_events_checks, a Saved table of the Project, holds the row count of each day of ops.job_events; a write that adds a grand total row to it is refused:

from references import mart
statement(
    INSERT_OVERWRITE(mart.job_events_checks),
    SELECT(AS(count_rows(), "row_count"), job_events.dt),
    FROM(job_events),
    WHERE(between(job_events.dt, "2026-09-18", "2026-09-24")),
    GROUP_BY(rollup(job_events.dt)),
)

Python stops with this message

ValueError:
  What happened:  INSERT_OVERWRITE(job_events_checks) writes rows made by GROUP_BY(rollup(job_events.dt)).
  Why it matters: Each subtotal row totals over rows written with it, with NULL in the columns it totals over: it can repeat the Key of a real row, and a sum over the Saved table would count each row more than once.
  Usual fix:      Write the plain GROUP_BY into the Saved table, and add the subtotals in the Statement that reads it.
  Opt-out:        none - this one can't be switched off.

Write the plain GROUP_BY(job_events.dt), as the table's notebook does, and add the subtotals in the Statement that reads the Saved table.

is_total in WHERE

WHERE picks the rows before GROUP_BY makes any subtotal, so there is none to test there:

statement(
    SELECT(job_owners.team, AS(count_rows(), "jobs")),
    FROM(job_owners),
    WHERE(equals(job_owners.dt, "2026-09-24"), is_total(job_owners.team)),
    GROUP_BY(rollup(job_owners.team)),
)

Python stops with this message

ValueError:
  What happened:  WHERE has is_total(job_owners.team).
  Why it matters: GROUP_BY makes the subtotal rows after WHERE has picked the rows, so there is none to test in WHERE.
  Usual fix:      Test it in HAVING, or show it in SELECT, such as AS(if_else(is_total(job_owners.team), 1, 0), "is_subtotal").
  Opt-out:        none - this one can't be switched off.

Test it in HAVING, as Keep only the subtotals does.

16. Check data quality with Statements Intermediate

Goal

Check a table's data before you trust a number built on it, with Statements you keep and run again: Keys that repeat, NULLs in each column, the rows in each Partition, and two tables that should agree. Then run them all at once and gather what they find in one pandas DataFrame, and see where the Project keeps such checks: a Table notebook made from the quality_checks Template.

When you'd use it

Before you build on a table that is new to you, after a load that looked odd, or every morning before the Project's Saved tables are written. A check that is a Statement runs on the warehouse, so it reads every row of the Partitions you give it, and your notebook gets back only the few rows that matter.

It needs the Getting started how-tos Count, join and stay safe and Save a table.

Steps

Start from the Intermediate Example project

Work in a copy of the Intermediate Example project, at its top: copy example_projects/intermediate/ from the download to a folder of your own, copy the sqlglot_composer folder into it, as a Project holds it, and open a notebook there. This page makes the same copy in its first step, from the download the Toolbox came in, and runs its steps there:

import shutil
from pathlib import Path
import sqlglot_composer
download = Path(sqlglot_composer.__file__).parents[1]  # -> Path
_ = shutil.copytree(download / "example_projects" / "intermediate", ".", dirs_exist_ok=True)

Then import the Toolbox, pandas, the project module, the Project's ops Database and your query. This how-to reads three of its tables, each holding 14 days, 2026-09-11 to 2026-09-24: ops.job_owners, which says each day who owns each job; ops.job_events, each run's start, finish, retry or fail; and ops.region_costs, what each job cost per region and day, in cents, which writes its days like 20260911, not 2026-09-11, so its days are written that way below.

from sqlglot_composer import *
from sqlglot_composer import project
import pandas as pd
from references import ops
from warehouse import query, execute
job_owners = ops.job_owners  # -> Table
job_events = ops.job_events  # -> Table
region_costs = ops.region_costs  # -> Table
Find Keys that repeat

A Table reference's Key lists the columns that pick out one row of the table. For ops.job_owners it is job_owners.job_id and job_owners.dt: one row per job per day. The warehouse never enforces a Key, and JOIN relies on it to warn you about repeated rows, so check it holds.

Write a check so that each row it gives back is a problem. Here, group the rows by the Key and keep, with HAVING, only the groups holding more than one row:

repeated_keys = statement(  # -> Statement
    SELECT(job_owners.job_id, job_owners.dt, AS(count_rows(), "copies")),
    FROM(job_owners),
    WHERE(between(job_owners.dt, "2026-09-11", "2026-09-24")),
    GROUP_BY(job_owners.job_id, job_owners.dt),
    HAVING(more_than(count_rows(), 1)),
)
run_query(repeated_keys, query)  # -> DataFrame

Python shows

No rows.

No rows: no Key repeats on any of the 14 days. The Toolbox's own check_key does the same for the rows its where= picks, and says so in a sentence:

check_key(job_owners, query=query,  # -> Verdict
          where=between(job_owners.dt, "2026-09-11", "2026-09-24"))

Python shows

ops.job_owners: the key (job_id, dt) holds where job_owners.dt BETWEEN '2026-09-11' AND '2026-09-24'.
Count the NULLs in every column

all_columns gives every column of a Table reference, in a list, so one short function writes a NULL count for each column of any table. A column's text is the Hive that names it, such as job_owners.owner, and the part after the dot is its own name, which names each count. Which rows to count is a condition on one of the table's partition columns, since each table is partitioned its own way:

def null_counts(t: Table, where: Condition) -> Statement:
    counts = [AS(count_rows(where=is_null(column)), "null_" + str(column).split(".")[1])
              for column in all_columns(t)]
    return statement(
        SELECT(AS(count_rows(), "total_rows"), counts),
        FROM(t),
        WHERE(where),
    )

Here is the Hive it writes for ops.job_owners, one count per column:

owner_nulls = null_counts(  # -> Statement
    job_owners, between(job_owners.dt, "2026-09-11", "2026-09-24"))
text = show_hive(owner_nulls)  # -> str

Hive, ready to paste

SELECT
  COUNT(*) AS total_rows,
  COUNT(CASE WHEN job_owners.job_id IS NULL THEN 1 END) AS null_job_id,
  COUNT(CASE WHEN job_owners.team IS NULL THEN 1 END) AS null_team,
  COUNT(CASE WHEN job_owners.owner IS NULL THEN 1 END) AS null_owner,
  COUNT(CASE WHEN job_owners.dt IS NULL THEN 1 END) AS null_dt
FROM ops.job_owners AS job_owners
WHERE
  job_owners.dt BETWEEN '2026-09-11' AND '2026-09-24';
run_query(owner_nulls, query)  # -> DataFrame

    FROM(job_events),
    WHERE(between(job_events.dt, "2026-09-11", "2026-09-24")),

Check that two tables agree

Every run that starts should get a bill. ops.job_events says how many runs started each day, and ops.region_costs how many bills came in. Count each, per day, with one Statement each:

starts_per_day = statement(  # -> Statement
    SELECT(job_events.dt,
           AS(count_rows(where=equals(job_events.event_type, "start")), "starts")),
    FROM(job_events),
    WHERE(between(job_events.dt, "2026-09-11", "2026-09-24")),
    GROUP_BY(job_events.dt),
)
bills_per_day = statement(  # -> Statement
    SELECT(region_costs.dt,
           AS(count_rows(where=is_not_null(region_costs.cost_cents)), "bills")),
    FROM(region_costs),
    WHERE(between(region_costs.dt, "20260911", "20260924")),
    GROUP_BY(region_costs.dt),
)

The two tables write their days differently, so compare the two small results in pandas: write region_costs's days like job_events's, then put the two side by side with starts.merge. how="outer" keeps a day that only one of them has, with NaN, pandas' empty value, for the other count, so that day shows up as a difference too:

starts = run_query(starts_per_day, query)  # -> DataFrame
bills = run_query(bills_per_day, query)  # -> DataFrame
bills["dt"] = pd.to_datetime(bills["dt"], format="%Y%m%d").dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
both = starts.merge(bills, on="dt", how="outer")  # -> DataFrame
both[both["starts"] != both["bills"]]

Python shows

On 2026-09-24 two runs started but only one was billed: invoice_sync is still running, and its bill comes in when it finishes.

Run every check and gather what they find

Two more checks, each giving the rows that are problems: jobs with no owner on the newest day, and costs not billed yet:

no_owner = statement(  # -> Statement
    SELECT(job_owners.job_id, job_owners.dt),
    FROM(job_owners),
    WHERE(equals(job_owners.dt, "2026-09-24"), is_null(job_owners.owner)),
)
not_billed = statement(  # -> Statement
    SELECT(region_costs.job_id, region_costs.region, region_costs.dt),
    FROM(region_costs),
    WHERE(between(region_costs.dt, "20260911", "20260924"),
          is_null(region_costs.cost_cents)),
)

Keep the checks in a dict, by name, and run each in a loop. Add the days on which the two tables disagree, already in pandas, then count each check's problem rows:

checks = {"repeated_keys": repeated_keys, "no_owner": no_owner,
          "not_billed": not_billed}
found = {name: run_query(check_statement, query)  # -> dict[str, DataFrame]
         for name, check_statement in checks.items()}
found["starts_not_billed"] = both[both["starts"] != both["bills"]]
summary = pd.DataFrame({"check": list(found),  # -> DataFrame
                        "problem_rows": [len(rows) for rows in found.values()]})
summary

Keep a table's checks in its own Table notebook

The Project keeps the checks it runs every day in a Table notebook made from the quality_checks Template: project.new_table("mart.job_events_checks", template="quality_checks") made tables/mart__job_events_checks/mart__job_events_checks.ipynb. Its logic cell names the rows it checks once, as READS, the newest day of ops.job_events, and defines a check of repeated Keys and a NULL count, as above, beside a checks_logic.write() that saves each day's row count, so a day that came in short shows beside the days around it. project.load gives its functions:

checks_logic = project.load("mart.job_events_checks")  # -> the notebook's functions

Each check you expect to pass gives no rows, and each one that finds something names the rows you can explain: no_owner names cache_warm, job 4, which has never had an owner, and not_billed names invoice_sync, job 2, still running on 2026-09-24.

Common mistakes

Looking for NULLs with equals

In SQL nothing equals NULL, not even NULL, so a condition owner = NULL matches no row, and the count comes out 0 however many owners are missing. The Toolbox refuses it as you build it:

count_rows(where=equals(job_owners.owner, None))

Python stops with this message

GuardRefused:
  What happened:  equals(job_owners.owner, None) compares with None.
  Why it matters: In SQL nothing is equal to NULL, not even NULL, so this would match no rows and quietly give an empty or wrong result.
  Usual fix:      Use is_null(column) or is_not_null(column) to find missing values.
  Opt-out:        none - this one can't be switched off.

Use is_null(column), as null_counts does, or is_not_null(column).

Expecting a day with no rows to show 0

GROUP_BY makes one row per value it finds, so a day with no rows at all isn't in the result: it doesn't show with 0. invoice_sync, job 2, runs on weekdays only, and its count per day skips the weekends without a word:

invoice_sync_per_day = statement(  # -> Statement
    SELECT(job_events.dt, AS(count_rows(), "events")),
    FROM(job_events),
    WHERE(between(job_events.dt, "2026-09-11", "2026-09-24"),
          equals(job_events.job_id, 2)),
    GROUP_BY(job_events.dt),
)
per_day = run_query(invoice_sync_per_day, query)  # -> DataFrame
len(per_day)

Python shows

10

To find the days that are missing, list every day you expected, with pd.date_range, and keep those the result doesn't hold:

every_day = pd.date_range("2026-09-11", "2026-09-24").strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
[day for day in every_day if day not in set(per_day["dt"])]

Python shows

['2026-09-12', '2026-09-13', '2026-09-19', '2026-09-20']

Here the four are weekends, as expected. A missing weekday would be a load to look into.

A check that reads every Partition

A check of a partitioned table must filter one of its partition columns, as any read must. A NULL count over all of ops.region_costs is refused, naming its partition columns:

statement(SELECT(AS(count_rows(where=is_null(region_costs.cost_cents)), "nulls")),
          FROM(region_costs))

Python stops with this message

LoadRefused:
  What happened:  FROM(region_costs) reads ops.region_costs, but filters none of its partition columns: region, dt.
  Why it matters: The warehouse would read every Partition the table holds, which can stall the cluster for everyone.
  Usual fix:      Filter one of them in WHERE, as in WHERE(equals(region_costs.region, ...)), or with is_in, between or last_n_days.
  Opt-out:        FROM(region_costs, reads_all_partitions=True)

Give each check the Partitions it checks, as null_counts takes them in where.

  • Put two tables' rows side by side, and find the ones that differ: Reconcile two tables.
  • The gallery's check_table_reference checks that a Table reference still matches its table, and check_key checks its Key on the rows you pick.

Toolbox names used: Table, check_key, all_columns, SELECT, AS, FROM, WHERE, GROUP_BY, HAVING, statement, Statement, equals, is_null, is_not_null, more_than, between, Condition, count_rows, show_hive, run_query, project.load

17. Call other Hive functions Intermediate

Goal

Call a Hive function the Toolbox has no function of its own for, such as upper or concat, with hive_function. Then see three things worth knowing about the Hive the Toolbox writes: what a division by 0 gives, how a Python float is written, and a function written by another name.

When you'd use it

When the Hive you need has a function the Toolbox doesn't wrap: text functions such as upper, concat or substr, or date functions such as datediff and date_format. And when the Hive you see isn't quite what you typed.

It needs the Getting started how-tos Build and run a first statement and Count, join and stay safe.

Then import the Toolbox, the Project's ops Database and your query:

from sqlglot_composer import *
from references import ops
from warehouse import query, execute
job_owners = ops.job_owners  # -> Table
job_events = ops.job_events  # -> Table
Call a function the Toolbox doesn't wrap

hive_function takes the function's name as text, then its arguments: columns, or values, which it quotes for you. It gives back a Column, a calculation to name with AS. Here upper writes each team in capitals, and concat joins each job's owner and team into one contact, such as ana@data:

contacts = statement(  # -> Statement
    SELECT(job_owners.job_id,
           AS(hive_function("upper", job_owners.team), "team"),
           AS(hive_function("concat", fill_null(job_owners.owner, "nobody"), "@",
                            job_owners.team), "contact")),
    FROM(job_owners),
    WHERE(equals(job_owners.dt, "2026-09-24")),
)
text = show_hive(contacts)  # -> str

Hive, ready to paste

SELECT
  job_owners.job_id,
  UPPER(job_owners.team) AS team,
  CONCAT(COALESCE(job_owners.owner, 'nobody'), '@', job_owners.team) AS contact
FROM ops.job_owners AS job_owners
WHERE
  job_owners.dt = '2026-09-24';
run_query(contacts, query)  # -> DataFrame

Python shows

job_idteamcontact
1DATAana@data
2FINANCEben@finance
3FINANCEchloe@finance
4WEBnobody@web

The function concat gives NULL as soon as one of its arguments is NULL, so fill_null puts "nobody" in where a job has no owner, as job 4, cache_warm, has none.

Before writing the call, hive_function checks it: for the functions it knows, such as upper, substr or date_add, it refuses the wrong number of arguments, and it refuses a function that works only over a window of rows, such as lag or rank. The Common mistakes below show both.

Three things to know about the Hive

Each step below builds a Statement, shows the Hive the Toolbox writes for it, and runs it.

Dividing by something that could be 0

How many retries each job's finished runs needed on 2026-09-24: the retries, divided by the finishes.

retries_per_finish = statement(  # -> Statement
    SELECT(job_events.job_id,
           AS(count_rows(where=equals(job_events.event_type, "retry"))
              / count_rows(where=equals(job_events.event_type, "finish")),
              "retries_per_finish")),
    FROM(job_events),
    WHERE(equals(job_events.dt, "2026-09-24")),
    GROUP_BY(job_events.job_id),
)
text = show_hive(retries_per_finish)  # -> str

Hive, ready to paste

SELECT
  job_events.job_id,
  COUNT(CASE WHEN job_events.event_type = 'retry' THEN 1 END) / COUNT(CASE WHEN job_events.event_type = 'finish' THEN 1 END) AS retries_per_finish
FROM ops.job_events AS job_events
WHERE
  job_events.dt = '2026-09-24'
GROUP BY
  job_events.job_id;
run_query(retries_per_finish, query)  # -> DataFrame

Python shows

job_idretries_per_finish
10.0
2NULL

invoice_sync, job 2, is still running on 2026-09-24, so it has no finish, and its row divides by 0. Hive gives that row NULL, which pandas shows as NaN, rather than stop.

A Python float

The jobs whose finished runs took more than 15.5 minutes on average. job_events.minutes holds the minutes since the run started, so on a "finish" row it is how long the run took. 15.5 is a Python float:

long_runs = statement(  # -> Statement
    SELECT(job_events.job_id, AS(count_rows(), "finished_runs")),
    FROM(job_events),
    WHERE(between(job_events.dt, "2026-09-11", "2026-09-24"),
          equals(job_events.event_type, "finish")),
    GROUP_BY(job_events.job_id),
    HAVING(more_than(average_of(job_events.minutes), 15.5)),
)
text = show_hive(long_runs)  # -> str

Hive, ready to paste

SELECT
  job_events.job_id,
  COUNT(*) AS finished_runs
FROM ops.job_events AS job_events
WHERE
  job_events.dt BETWEEN '2026-09-11' AND '2026-09-24'
  AND job_events.event_type = 'finish'
GROUP BY
  job_events.job_id
HAVING
  AVG(job_events.minutes) > 15.5;
run_query(long_runs, query)  # -> DataFrame

Python shows

job_idfinished_runs
29
33

A Python float is written as it is, 15.5, which Hive reads as a DOUBLE, SQL's float.

A hive_function call written by another name

The function nvl gives its first argument, or its second where the first is NULL, as fill_null does. Here it puts "none" in for cache_warm, job 4, which has no owner:

owners = statement(  # -> Statement
    SELECT(job_owners.job_id, AS(hive_function("nvl", job_owners.owner, "none"), "owner")),
    FROM(job_owners),
    WHERE(equals(job_owners.dt, "2026-09-24")),
)
text = show_hive(owners)  # -> str

Hive, ready to paste

SELECT
  job_owners.job_id,
  COALESCE(job_owners.owner, 'none') AS owner
FROM ops.job_owners AS job_owners
WHERE
  job_owners.dt = '2026-09-24';
run_query(owners, query)  # -> DataFrame

Python shows

job_idowner
1ana
2ben
3chloe
4none

The Hive says COALESCE, not nvl: the Toolbox writes a hive_function call as sqlglot reads it back, sometimes by another name that does the same, as COALESCE for nvl, and sometimes with an argument changed, as the Common mistakes below show for date_format. The result is the same.

Check it worked

The function's name, in capitals, and each argument are in the Hive, and the result holds what the function gives: every team in capitals, and a contact for every job.

result = run_query(contacts, query)  # -> DataFrame
list(result["team"])

Python shows

['DATA', 'FINANCE', 'FINANCE', 'WEB']
int(result["contact"].isna().sum())

Python shows

0

int(...) makes the count a plain number, which numpy would otherwise print as np.int64(0).

Common mistakes

A column's name as text

hive_function quotes text for you, so "team" is the word team, not the column. Every row gets the same value, and nothing stops it:

shouting = statement(  # -> Statement
    SELECT(job_owners.job_id, AS(hive_function("upper", "team"), "team")),
    FROM(job_owners),
    WHERE(equals(job_owners.dt, "2026-09-24")),
)
run_query(shouting, query)  # -> DataFrame

Python shows

job_idteam
1TEAM
2TEAM
3TEAM
4TEAM

Pass the column itself, job_owners.team, as the steps do.

The whole call written as text

Only the function's name is text; its arguments go after it, one by one:

hive_function("upper(job_owners.team)")

Python stops with this message

ValueError:
  What happened:  hive_function('upper(job_owners.team)', ...) isn't a function name.
  Why it matters: Only the function's name is written as it is, so it must be a plain name: letters, digits and _.
  Usual fix:      Use the Hive function's name, such as hive_function("upper", jobs.team).
  Opt-out:        none - this one can't be switched off.
The wrong number of arguments

The function substr needs the text and where to start, and takes how many characters as a third, if you want it. Given one, the warehouse would stop, so the Toolbox refuses it first:

hive_function("substr", job_owners.owner)

Python stops with this message

TypeError:
  What happened:  hive_function('substr', ...) gives substr 1 argument, and substr takes 2 to 3 arguments.
  Why it matters: The warehouse would stop the whole Statement with an error when it runs.
  Usual fix:      Give hive_function 2 to 3 arguments after "substr".
  Opt-out:        none - this one can't be switched off.
A NULL in concat

Without fill_null, a job with no owner gets no contact at all, not "@web":

no_fill = statement(  # -> Statement
    SELECT(job_owners.job_id,
           AS(hive_function("concat", job_owners.owner, "@", job_owners.team),
              "contact")),
    FROM(job_owners),
    WHERE(equals(job_owners.dt, "2026-09-24")),
)
run_query(no_fill, query)  # -> DataFrame

Python shows

job_idcontact
1ana@data
2ben@finance
3chloe@finance
4NULL
YYYY for the year in date_format

In a date_format pattern, write yyyy for the year. YYYY is the year a week belongs to, which differs from the year in the last days of December and the first of January.

by_month = statement(  # -> Statement
    SELECT(job_events.event_id,
           AS(hive_function("date_format", job_events.dt, "YYYY-MM"), "month")),
    FROM(job_events),
    WHERE(equals(job_events.dt, "2026-09-24")),
)

No message stops you: the Toolbox writes the pattern as sqlglot reads it back, here as yyyy-MM, which is what you meant. Write yyyy anyway, so your Python says what its Hive does.

text = show_hive(by_month)  # -> str

Hive, ready to paste

SELECT
  job_events.event_id,
  DATE_FORMAT(job_events.dt, 'yyyy-MM') AS month
FROM ops.job_events AS job_events
WHERE
  job_events.dt = '2026-09-24';
A function that works over a window of rows

lag, lead, rank and the other window functions need OVER (...) after them, which hive_function can't write, so it refuses them. For lag, lead, rank, dense_rank, ntile and row_number, its message names the Toolbox's own function that writes it, such as lag, which takes a window; for the others, such as percent_rank, it says to work it out in pandas. Look across rows shows the ones the Toolbox writes.

Next

  • lag, rank and a rolling sum, each over a Window: Look across rows.
  • Hive written by hand, beside your Table references, where no Toolbox function fits: Hand-written Hive with your Table references.
  • The gallery's hive_function entry, and fill_null for putting a value in where a column is NULL.

Toolbox names used: SELECT, AS, FROM, WHERE, GROUP_BY, HAVING, statement, equals, more_than, between, count_rows, average_of, fill_null, hive_function, show_hive, run_query

18. Look across rows, then finish in pandas Intermediate

Goal

Work out on the warehouse what looks across the rows around each row: each row's value from the row before it (lag), a rank within each group (rank), a rolling sum, and a group's total beside each row, each over a window. Keep only some of those rows through a Derived table, and write a Partition of a Saved table that looks back on earlier ones. Then finish in pandas: put the results of several Statements side by side with a merge.

When you'd use it

When a step needs the rows around each row, written OVER (...) in SQL: how a run compares with the one before it, a running or moving total, a rank. A window says which rows: the rows of each group, in an order, and with rows= only those near each row. The warehouse does that work, reading every row of the Partitions you give it, and hands back the result. And when the numbers you need come from Statements on different tables, small enough to combine in your notebook, pandas finishes the job.

It needs the Getting started how-tos Count, join and stay safe, Share Building blocks, which starts with Derived tables, and Save a table.

Then import the Toolbox, pandas, the project module, the Project's ops Database and your query and execute:

from sqlglot_composer import *
from sqlglot_composer import project
import pandas as pd
from references import ops
from warehouse import query, execute
job_events = ops.job_events  # -> Table
region_costs = ops.region_costs  # -> Table
Name the Window

A Window names the rows each row looks across. PARTITION_BY= makes the groups, here each job: the word is SQL's, and has nothing to do with a table's Partitions. ORDER_BY= puts each group's rows in order, here by day. Each job finishes at most once a day in the Example database, so ordering by day gives each job's runs one clear order.

each_jobs_runs = window(  # -> Window
    PARTITION_BY=job_events.job_id, ORDER_BY=job_events.dt)

And the rows to read, the same in every step: the finished runs of the last week of the Example database.

week_finished = [  # -> list[Condition]
    between(job_events.dt, "2026-09-18", "2026-09-24"),
    equals(job_events.event_type, "finish"),
]
The run before: lag

How much faster or slower was each run than the job's run before it? lag gives each row the value of the row before it in its Window's order, and NULL to the first row of each job. pandas holds a missing number as NaN, and so shows that column with decimals; the tables on this page show NaN as NULL:

with_before = statement(  # -> Statement
    SELECT(job_events.job_id, job_events.dt, job_events.minutes,
           AS(lag(job_events.minutes, over=each_jobs_runs), "minutes_before"),
           AS(job_events.minutes - lag(job_events.minutes, over=each_jobs_runs), "change")),
    FROM(job_events),
    WHERE(*week_finished),
)
text = show_hive(with_before)  # -> str

Hive, ready to paste

SELECT
  job_events.job_id,
  job_events.dt,
  job_events.minutes,
  LAG(job_events.minutes, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY job_events.job_id ORDER BY job_events.dt ASC) AS minutes_before,
  job_events.minutes - LAG(job_events.minutes, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY job_events.job_id ORDER BY job_events.dt ASC) AS change
FROM ops.job_events AS job_events
WHERE
  job_events.dt BETWEEN '2026-09-18' AND '2026-09-24'
  AND job_events.event_type = 'finish';
run_query(with_before, query)  # -> DataFrame

Python shows

job_iddtminutesminutes_beforechange
12026-09-1814NULLNULL
12026-09-191114.0-3.0
12026-09-201211.01.0
12026-09-211312.01.0
12026-09-221013.0-3.0
12026-09-231210.02.0
12026-09-241012.0-2.0
22026-09-1822NULLNULL
22026-09-212122.0-1.0
22026-09-221821.0-3.0
22026-09-231818.00.0
32026-09-2133NULLNULL

The Window sees only the rows the Statement reads: job 1 ran on 2026-09-17 too, but WHERE starts on 2026-09-18, so its run on 2026-09-18 has no run before it.

A rank within each group: rank

Which of each job's runs took longest? rank numbers each job's runs in its Window's order, here the longest first, with descending. Two runs that tie get the same rank, and the next run the rank after both, as job 1's two runs of 12 minutes do: both 3, then 5 for its run of 11 minutes:

longest_first = window(PARTITION_BY=job_events.job_id,  # -> Window
                       ORDER_BY=descending(job_events.minutes))
ranked = statement(  # -> Statement
    SELECT(job_events.job_id, job_events.dt, job_events.minutes,
           AS(rank(over=longest_first), "longest_first")),
    FROM(job_events),
    WHERE(*week_finished),
)
run_query(ranked, query)  # -> DataFrame

dense_rank gives a tie the same rank too, but the next rank follows straight on: 3, 3, then 4. To keep each job's one newest run, or its top N, use row_number, which never ties: see The latest row of each group, and the top N.

A rolling sum, and a group's total beside each row

The minutes of each job's last three runs, added up, beside the job's minutes for the week. sum_of(..., over=...) adds up each row's Window, and gives each row its own total. rows=(-2, 0) keeps only the two rows before each row and the row itself; with no ORDER_BY and no rows=, the Window is the whole job:

last_three = statement(  # -> Statement
    SELECT(job_events.job_id, job_events.dt, job_events.minutes,
           AS(sum_of(job_events.minutes, over=window(
               PARTITION_BY=job_events.job_id, ORDER_BY=job_events.dt, rows=(-2, 0))),
              "last_3_runs"),
           AS(sum_of(job_events.minutes, over=window(PARTITION_BY=job_events.job_id)),
              "week_minutes")),
    FROM(job_events),
    WHERE(*week_finished),
)
text = show_hive(last_three)  # -> str

Hive, ready to paste

SELECT
  job_events.job_id,
  job_events.dt,
  job_events.minutes,
  SUM(job_events.minutes) OVER (
    PARTITION BY job_events.job_id
    ORDER BY job_events.dt ASC
    ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS last_3_runs,
  SUM(job_events.minutes) OVER (PARTITION BY job_events.job_id) AS week_minutes
FROM ops.job_events AS job_events
WHERE
  job_events.dt BETWEEN '2026-09-18' AND '2026-09-24'
  AND job_events.event_type = 'finish';
run_query(last_three, query)  # -> DataFrame

Keep only some rows: through a Derived table

Which runs were slower than the job's run before? Hive works a Window out after it picks the rows, so a test on "change" can't go in the WHERE of the Statement that works it out (see Common mistakes). Name that Statement with derived, and test it in the Statement that reads it:

changes = derived("changes", with_before)  # -> Table
slower = statement(  # -> Statement
    SELECT(changes.job_id, changes.dt, changes.change),
    FROM(changes),
    WHERE(more_than(changes.change, 0)),
)
run_query(slower, query)  # -> DataFrame

Write a Partition that looks back on earlier ones

To keep each run's change in a Saved table, a day's Partition at a time, each day's write needs the runs before it, which may be on earlier days. So read the earlier days too in a Derived table that keeps the day column, and keep only the day written in the Statement that writes, with WHERE(equals(week.dt, day)), naming its Partition with partition={"dt": day}. Read only the day itself, and each job's first run that day would have no run before it.

The Saved table, mart.run_changes, has a Table reference of its own, written by hand as Describe a table by hand shows, and registered:

The file references/mart__run_changes.py, after you write it

"""mart.run_changes - each finished run beside the job's run before."""
from sqlglot_composer import Table

run_changes = Table(
    "mart.run_changes",
    columns={
        "event_id": "bigint",
        "job_id": "bigint",
        "minutes": "int",
        "minutes_before": "int",  # the job's run before; NULL for its first
        "dt": "string",
    },
    partitioned_by=["dt"],
    key=["event_id", "dt"],
    location="/data/your_team/mart.db/run_changes",
    purge=True,
)
_ = project.register("mart.run_changes")

"""mart - a Database: written by the Project actions, never by hand.

Why: `from references import mart` gives each of its Table references by its name, so a column
is reached as mart.budget_overruns.job_id.

Its tables: budget_overruns (references/mart__budget_overruns.py), job_day_costs
(references/mart__job_day_costs.py), job_day_facts (references/mart__job_day_facts.py),
job_events_checks (references/mart__job_events_checks.py), job_notes
(references/mart__job_notes.py), run_changes (references/mart__run_changes.py), team_days
(references/mart__team_days.py), team_failures (references/mart__team_failures.py).

The Project actions and refresh_reference_sheet write this file again from the Table
references in references/, so a change made here is lost. A Table reference with a <...> still
in it, as new_table writes one, is left out until it is filled in.
"""

import difflib
from typing import NoReturn

from references.mart__budget_overruns import budget_overruns
from references.mart__job_day_costs import job_day_costs
from references.mart__job_day_facts import job_day_facts
from references.mart__job_events_checks import job_events_checks
from references.mart__job_notes import job_notes
from references.mart__run_changes import run_changes
from references.mart__team_days import team_days
from references.mart__team_failures import team_failures

# Its tables, by the names tab completion lists and a wrong name's message gives: the names
# `from references.mart import *` gives, too.
__all__ = ["budget_overruns", "job_day_costs", "job_day_facts", "job_events_checks", "job_notes", "run_changes", "team_days", "team_failures"]
_TABLES = __all__


def __getattr__(name: str) -> NoReturn:
    """A name that isn't one of its tables: say which tables it has, and the closest."""
    if name.startswith("_"):
        raise AttributeError(name)
    close = difflib.get_close_matches(name, _TABLES, n=1)
    hint = f" Did you mean {close[0]!r}?" if close else ""
    raise AttributeError(f"mart has no table {name!r}.{hint} Its tables are: "
                         f"{', '.join(_TABLES)}.", obj=None)


def __dir__() -> list[str]:
    """Its tables, so tab completion lists them."""
    return list(_TABLES)

It writes admin/registry.csv too.

from references.mart__run_changes import run_changes

Here a job's run before may be up to 6 days back, so each write reads its day and the 6 before it:

import datetime
def changes_on(day: str) -> Statement:
    week_before = (datetime.date.fromisoformat(day)
                   - datetime.timedelta(days=6)).isoformat()
    week = derived("week", statement(
        SELECT(job_events.event_id, job_events.job_id, job_events.dt, job_events.minutes,
               AS(lag(job_events.minutes, over=each_jobs_runs), "minutes_before")),
        FROM(job_events),
        WHERE(between(job_events.dt, week_before, day),
              equals(job_events.event_type, "finish")),
    ))
    return statement(
        INSERT_OVERWRITE(run_changes, partition={"dt": day}),
        SELECT(week.event_id, week.job_id, week.minutes, week.minutes_before),
        FROM(week),
        WHERE(equals(week.dt, day)),
    )
text = show_hive(changes_on("2026-09-24"))  # -> str

Hive, ready to paste

WITH week AS (
  SELECT
    job_events.event_id,
    job_events.job_id,
    job_events.dt,
    job_events.minutes,
    LAG(job_events.minutes, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY job_events.job_id ORDER BY job_events.dt ASC) AS minutes_before
  FROM ops.job_events AS job_events
  WHERE
    job_events.dt BETWEEN '2026-09-18' AND '2026-09-24'
    AND job_events.event_type = 'finish'
)
INSERT OVERWRITE TABLE mart.run_changes PARTITION(dt = '2026-09-24')
SELECT
  week.event_id,
  week.job_id,
  week.minutes,
  week.minutes_before
FROM week
WHERE
  week.dt = '2026-09-24';

Merge the results of several Statements

The cost of each minute a job ran comes from two tables: its minutes from ops.job_events, and its cost from ops.region_costs. Add up each per job, with a Statement each:

minutes_per_job = statement(  # -> Statement
    SELECT(job_events.job_id, AS(count_rows(), "runs"),
           AS(sum_of(job_events.minutes), "minutes")),
    FROM(job_events),
    WHERE(*week_finished),
    GROUP_BY(job_events.job_id),
)
cost_per_job = statement(  # -> Statement
    SELECT(region_costs.job_id, AS(sum_of(region_costs.cost_cents), "cost_cents")),
    FROM(region_costs),
    WHERE(between(region_costs.dt, "20260918", "20260924")),
    GROUP_BY(region_costs.job_id),
)
minutes = run_query(minutes_per_job, query)  # -> DataFrame
costs = run_query(cost_per_job, query)  # -> DataFrame

.merge puts the two side by side, matching rows on "job_id". how="outer" keeps a job that only one of them has, and validate="one_to_one" stops the merge if "job_id" repeats on either side, which would repeat rows:

per_job = minutes.merge(  # -> DataFrame
    costs, on="job_id", how="outer", validate="one_to_one")
per_job["cents_per_minute"] = (per_job["cost_cents"] / per_job["minutes"]).round(2)
per_job

report_build, job 3, costs most per minute: it finished once this week, but its run that failed on 2026-09-18 was billed too.

The Toolbox could join the two as Derived tables in one Statement, and on big results that is the way: the warehouse does the work. For two small results you already have, a merge in pandas is quicker to write and to change.

Common mistakes

Testing a Window's result in the same Statement

A Window is worked out after the rows are picked, so Hive can't test it in the WHERE of the Statement that works it out:

in_one_go = statement(
    SELECT(job_events.job_id, job_events.dt),
    FROM(job_events),
    WHERE(*week_finished,
          more_than(job_events.minutes - lag(job_events.minutes, over=each_jobs_runs), 0)),
)

Python stops with this message

ValueError:
  What happened:  WHERE has job_events.minutes - LAG(job_events.minutes, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY job_events.job_id ORDER BY job_events.dt ASC) > 0, which looks across rows through a Window.
  Why it matters: Windows are worked out last, after the rows are picked and grouped, so Hive can't use it in WHERE of the SELECT that makes it.
  Usual fix:      Work it out in a derived(...) table, then use it in the Statement that reads it; help(row_number) shows how.
  Opt-out:        none - this one can't be switched off.

Test it in the Statement that reads it as a Derived table, as the step Keep only some rows does.

A running total with ORDER_BY and no rows=
sum_of(job_events.minutes, over=each_jobs_runs)

Python stops with this message

ValueError:
  What happened:  sum_of(job_events.minutes) is given a Window with ORDER_BY and no rows=.
  Why it matters: Hive would work it out over the rows up to each row and every row tied with it in ORDER_BY's order, which is seldom what is meant, so say which rows.
  Usual fix:      Give rows=(None, 0) for a running total of every row up to each one, or rows=(-6, 0) for each row and the 6 before it; leave ORDER_BY out for the whole group's.
  Opt-out:        none - this one can't be switched off.

With ORDER_BY and no rows=, Hive would add up the rows up to each row and every row tied with it, which is seldom what's meant. Say which rows: rows=(None, 0) for every row up to each one, rows=(-2, 0) for the last three, or leave ORDER_BY out for the whole group.

Merging a result per day into one per job

Merge each job's week of minutes with its cost on each day, and each job's minutes repeat once per day, so adding them up gives far too much:

daily_cost = statement(  # -> Statement
    SELECT(region_costs.job_id, region_costs.dt, region_costs.cost_cents),
    FROM(region_costs),
    WHERE(between(region_costs.dt, "20260918", "20260924")),
)
daily_costs = run_query(daily_cost, query)  # -> DataFrame
repeated = minutes.merge(daily_costs, on="job_id")
int(repeated["minutes"].sum()), int(minutes["minutes"].sum())

Python shows

(1035, 194)

validate="one_to_one" stops such a merge rather than let it through:

minutes.merge(daily_costs, on="job_id", validate="one_to_one")

Python stops with this message

MergeError:
Merge keys are not unique in right dataset; not a one-to-one merge
Duplicates in right:
  job_id
      1
      1
      1
      1
      1 ...

Add up per job first, as cost_per_job does, then merge.

Next

  • Check that a Statement, and what you do in pandas after it, give the numbers you meant: Review and test a change.
  • Each job's last row, or its top N, kept with row_number: The latest row of each group.
  • Keys: a Window keeps every row, so a Statement's Key is its FROM table's; a row_number kept at 1 gives one row per group.
  • The gallery's window, lag and row_number entries.

Toolbox names used: SELECT, AS, FROM, WHERE, GROUP_BY, INSERT_OVERWRITE, statement, Statement, derived, equals, more_than, between, count_rows, sum_of, descending, window, rank, lag, show_hive, run_query, run_execute, project.register

19. Review and test a change Intermediate

Goal

Before you change a Building block that several Statements read, see what the change does to each of them, and check that they give the numbers you meant. Export their Lineage before the change and after it and compare the two Markdown files line by line; then work the same answer out a second way, in pandas, from the rows themselves, and compare the two with plain asserts.

When you'd use it

Before you change a Building block or a Table reference that other Statements rely on, when you review someone else's change, and before a Statement's numbers are read by other people. The lines that differ between the two Markdown files are what the change does, Statement by Statement, whatever the code looked like. The Toolbox's Guards and Warnings catch mistakes of a known shape, such as a join that repeats rows; only a test catches a Statement that counts the wrong thing.

It needs Share Building blocks, Save a table and Follow lineage.

Steps

Start from the Intermediate Example project

Work in a copy of the Intermediate Example project, at its top: copy example_projects/intermediate/ from the download to a folder of your own, copy the sqlglot_composer folder into it, as a Project holds it, and open a notebook there. This page makes the same copy in its first step, from the download the Toolbox came in, into the folder it runs in, which Python's path holds already, as Jupyter's does for a notebook's own folder:

import shutil
from pathlib import Path
import sqlglot_composer
download = Path(sqlglot_composer.__file__).parents[1]  # -> Path
_ = shutil.copytree(download / "example_projects" / "intermediate", ".", dirs_exist_ok=True)

import difflib
import pandas as pd

from sqlglot_composer import project

job_events, job_owners = ops.job_events, ops.job_owners  # -> Table, Table
The Building block and the Statements that read it

building_blocks/events_per_job.py is a Building block, as Share Building blocks shows: a Derived table of each job's events, runs and minutes per day. A run's minutes are on the event that ends it, finish or fail. Two notebooks read it: mart.job_day_facts saves its numbers, and mart.team_days checks a team's day from them.

project.load gives a Table notebook's logic, its functions, as project.run_tables reads them. A function of yours builds the two Statements from them, so after you change the Building block, one call builds them again; project.load reads the files as they are at that moment:

def build_statements(day: str) -> tuple[Statement, Statement]:
    facts = project.load("mart.job_day_facts")
    team_days = project.load("mart.team_days")
    return facts.write(), team_days.team_day_from_job_events(day)
facts_write, team_day = build_statements("2026-09-18")  # -> Statement, Statement
run_query(team_day, query)  # -> DataFrame

finance4234
A second answer, in pandas

Before changing anything, check that team_day gives the numbers you mean. Fetch the rows themselves, every column of every event of the day, and each job's team that day, and work the answer out in pandas, which counts in a way of its own. This is an oracle, an answer you trust because you can read each step of it:

def rows_of(day: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    events = run_query(statement(
        SELECT(all_columns(job_events)),
        FROM(job_events),
        WHERE(equals(job_events.dt, day)),
    ), query)
    teams = run_query(statement(
        SELECT(job_owners.job_id, job_owners.team),
        FROM(job_owners),
        WHERE(equals(job_owners.dt, day)),
    ), query)
    return events.merge(teams, on="job_id", how="left")
def oracle(rows: pd.DataFrame, ending: list[str]) -> pd.DataFrame:
    counted = rows.assign(
        started=rows["event_type"] == "start",
        ended=rows["minutes"].where(rows["event_type"].isin(ending), 0))
    return counted.groupby("team", as_index=False).agg(
        events=("event_id", "count"), runs=("started", "sum"), minutes=("ended", "sum"))
oracle(rows_of("2026-09-18"), ending=["finish", "fail"])  # -> DataFrame

Python shows

Fetching every row is fine for a test over a day or two; it is what the Statement saves you from on the whole table.

Compare the two with assert

assert stops with an AssertionError when what follows it is False, and does nothing when it is True. same_rows puts each DataFrame's rows in one order, by "team", and turns them into a list of plain dicts, which compare with == as Python lists do:

def same_rows(result: pd.DataFrame, expected: pd.DataFrame) -> bool:
    return (result.sort_values("team").to_dict("records")
            == expected.sort_values("team").to_dict("records"))
def test_team_day(s: Statement, day: str, ending: list[str]) -> None:
    result = run_query(s, query)
    expected = oracle(rows_of(day), ending)
    assert same_rows(result, expected), f"{day}:\n{result}\n{expected}"
test_team_day(team_day, "2026-09-18", ending=["finish", "fail"])

It printed nothing, so the assert held. Choose the days to hold the awkward cases: here 2026-09-18, when report_build failed, so a run ended without finishing.

## facts_write

It writes the Saved table mart.job_day_facts, replacing each partition its rows fill.

### Calculated columns

Every column that is calculated rather than copied, in the order it is calculated.

#### `events_per_job in facts_write.events`

Calculated in **events_per_job in facts_write** as `count_rows()`, which is `COUNT(*)`.

```text
events_per_job in facts_write.events = count_rows()
└─ (no columns: it counts rows)
```

Rows that count:
- WHERE in events_per_job in facts_write: `between(job_events.dt, "2026-09-22", "2026-09-24")`, which is `job_events.dt BETWEEN '2026-09-22' AND '2026-09-24'` (reads ops.job_events.dt)

One value for each different `job_events.job_id` and `job_events.dt`.

#### `events_per_job in facts_write.runs`

Calculated in **events_per_job in facts_write** as `count_rows(where=equals(job_events.event_type, "start"))`, which is `COUNT(CASE WHEN job_events.event_type = 'start' THEN 1 END)`.

```text
events_per_job in facts_write.runs = count_rows(where=equals(job_events.event_type, "start"))
└─ ops.job_events.event_type  (string)
```

Rows that count:
- WHERE in events_per_job in facts_write: `between(job_events.dt, "2026-09-22", "2026-09-24")`, which is `job_events.dt BETWEEN '2026-09-22' AND '2026-09-24'` (reads ops.job_events.dt)

One value for each different `job_events.job_id` and `job_events.dt`.

#### `events_per_job in facts_write.minutes`

Calculated in **events_per_job in facts_write** as `fill_null(sum_of(job_events.minutes, where=is_in(job_events.event_type, ["finish", "fail"])), 0)`, which is `COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN job_events.event_type IN ('finish', 'fail') THEN job_events.minutes END), 0)`.

```text
events_per_job in facts_write.minutes = fill_null(sum_of(job_events.minutes, where=is_in(job_events.event_type, ["finish", "fail"])), 0)
├─ ops.job_events.minutes  (int)
└─ ops.job_events.event_type  (string)
```

Rows that count:
- WHERE in events_per_job in facts_write: `between(job_events.dt, "2026-09-22", "2026-09-24")`, which is `job_events.dt BETWEEN '2026-09-22' AND '2026-09-24'` (reads ops.job_events.dt)

One value for each different `job_events.job_id` and `job_events.dt`.

### Copied columns

| Output | Comes from |
| --- | --- |
| `job_id` | events_per_job in facts_write.job_id ← ops.job_events.job_id |
| `team` | ops.job_owners.team |
| `events` | events_per_job in facts_write.events (calculated) |
| `runs` | events_per_job in facts_write.runs (calculated) ← ops.job_events.event_type |
| `minutes` | events_per_job in facts_write.minutes (calculated) ← ops.job_events.minutes |
| `dt` | events_per_job in facts_write.dt ← ops.job_events.dt |

### Keys

The columns that tell each step's rows apart, as the Toolbox works them out. A column in one is marked "in the Key" in the chart.

- derived('events_per_job', ...): Key (job_id, dt), since GROUP_BY makes one row for each job_id, dt.
- facts_write: Key (job_id, dt), since events_per_job's rows are told apart by job_id, dt.
- mart.job_day_facts' Key (job_id, dt) holds: each row written has its own.

### Hive as submitted

```sql
WITH events_per_job AS (
  SELECT
    job_events.job_id,
    job_events.dt,
    COUNT(*) AS events,
    COUNT(CASE WHEN job_events.event_type = 'start' THEN 1 END) AS runs,
    COALESCE(
      SUM(
        CASE WHEN job_events.event_type IN ('finish', 'fail') THEN job_events.minutes END
      ),
      0
    ) AS minutes
  FROM ops.job_events AS job_events
  WHERE
    job_events.dt BETWEEN '2026-09-22' AND '2026-09-24'
  GROUP BY
    job_events.job_id,
    job_events.dt
)
INSERT OVERWRITE TABLE mart.job_day_facts PARTITION(dt)
SELECT
  events_per_job.job_id,
  job_owners.team,
  events_per_job.events,
  events_per_job.runs,
  events_per_job.minutes,
  events_per_job.dt
FROM events_per_job
LEFT JOIN ops.job_owners AS job_owners
  ON job_owners.job_id = events_per_job.job_id
  AND job_owners.dt = events_per_job.dt
  AND job_owners.dt BETWEEN '2026-09-22' AND '2026-09-24'
```

Change the Building block

Say a failed run's minutes shouldn't count, only a finished run's: the minutes line of events_per_job changes, from where=ends_a_run, the Alias of a finish or a fail, to where=equals(job_events.event_type, "finish"), and its docstring and imports with it:

The file building_blocks/events_per_job.py, after you change it

"""events_per_job - each job's events, runs and minutes for each dt it reads.

Why: mart.job_day_facts saves these numbers, and mart.team_days' notebook checks a day from
them too, and writing them once here means the two always count them the same way.

A run's minutes are the minutes since it started, on its finish event: a run that failed
counts no minutes. A day with no run finishing has 0 minutes, not NULL.
"""

from sqlglot_composer import (
    AS, FROM, GROUP_BY, SELECT, WHERE, Table, between, count_rows, derived, equals,
    fill_null, statement, sum_of,
)
from references.ops__job_events import job_events


def events_per_job(first_day: str, last_day: str) -> Table:
    """One row per job and dt from first_day to last_day: its events, runs and minutes.

    The day, dt, ops.job_events' partition column, is kept in GROUP_BY, so each day's numbers
    stay apart when first_day and last_day are days apart, and in SELECT, so a Statement that
    reads this can join each row to another table on its day, and a write that reads it fills
    each day's Partition from it.
    """
    return derived(
        "events_per_job",
        statement(
            SELECT(
                job_events.job_id,
                job_events.dt,
                AS(count_rows(), "events"),
                AS(count_rows(where=equals(job_events.event_type, "start")), "runs"),
                AS(fill_null(sum_of(job_events.minutes, where=equals(job_events.event_type, "finish")), 0), "minutes"),
            ),
            FROM(job_events),
            WHERE(between(job_events.dt, first_day, last_day)),
            GROUP_BY(job_events.job_id, job_events.dt),
        ),
    )

Then build the Statements again, since each holds the Building block as it was when it was built, and export the Lineage after:

facts_write, team_day = build_statements("2026-09-18")
html_file, markdown_file = export_lineage(facts_write, team_day,
                                          to="after.html")  # -> tuple[Path, Path]

## facts_write

It writes the Saved table mart.job_day_facts, replacing each partition its rows fill.

### Calculated columns

Every column that is calculated rather than copied, in the order it is calculated.

#### `events_per_job in facts_write.events`

Calculated in **events_per_job in facts_write** as `count_rows()`, which is `COUNT(*)`.

```text
events_per_job in facts_write.events = count_rows()
└─ (no columns: it counts rows)
```

Rows that count:
- WHERE in events_per_job in facts_write: `between(job_events.dt, "2026-09-22", "2026-09-24")`, which is `job_events.dt BETWEEN '2026-09-22' AND '2026-09-24'` (reads ops.job_events.dt)

One value for each different `job_events.job_id` and `job_events.dt`.

#### `events_per_job in facts_write.runs`

Calculated in **events_per_job in facts_write** as `count_rows(where=equals(job_events.event_type, "start"))`, which is `COUNT(CASE WHEN job_events.event_type = 'start' THEN 1 END)`.

```text
events_per_job in facts_write.runs = count_rows(where=equals(job_events.event_type, "start"))
└─ ops.job_events.event_type  (string)
```

Rows that count:
- WHERE in events_per_job in facts_write: `between(job_events.dt, "2026-09-22", "2026-09-24")`, which is `job_events.dt BETWEEN '2026-09-22' AND '2026-09-24'` (reads ops.job_events.dt)

One value for each different `job_events.job_id` and `job_events.dt`.

#### `events_per_job in facts_write.minutes`

Calculated in **events_per_job in facts_write** as `fill_null(sum_of(job_events.minutes, where=equals(job_events.event_type, "finish")), 0)`, which is `COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN job_events.event_type = 'finish' THEN job_events.minutes END), 0)`.

```text
events_per_job in facts_write.minutes = fill_null(sum_of(job_events.minutes, where=equals(job_events.event_type, "finish")), 0)
├─ ops.job_events.minutes  (int)
└─ ops.job_events.event_type  (string)
```

Rows that count:
- WHERE in events_per_job in facts_write: `between(job_events.dt, "2026-09-22", "2026-09-24")`, which is `job_events.dt BETWEEN '2026-09-22' AND '2026-09-24'` (reads ops.job_events.dt)

One value for each different `job_events.job_id` and `job_events.dt`.

### Copied columns

| Output | Comes from |
| --- | --- |
| `job_id` | events_per_job in facts_write.job_id ← ops.job_events.job_id |
| `team` | ops.job_owners.team |
| `events` | events_per_job in facts_write.events (calculated) |
| `runs` | events_per_job in facts_write.runs (calculated) ← ops.job_events.event_type |
| `minutes` | events_per_job in facts_write.minutes (calculated) ← ops.job_events.minutes |
| `dt` | events_per_job in facts_write.dt ← ops.job_events.dt |

### Keys

The columns that tell each step's rows apart, as the Toolbox works them out. A column in one is marked "in the Key" in the chart.

- derived('events_per_job', ...): Key (job_id, dt), since GROUP_BY makes one row for each job_id, dt.
- facts_write: Key (job_id, dt), since events_per_job's rows are told apart by job_id, dt.
- mart.job_day_facts' Key (job_id, dt) holds: each row written has its own.

### Hive as submitted

```sql
WITH events_per_job AS (
  SELECT
    job_events.job_id,
    job_events.dt,
    COUNT(*) AS events,
    COUNT(CASE WHEN job_events.event_type = 'start' THEN 1 END) AS runs,
    COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN job_events.event_type = 'finish' THEN job_events.minutes END), 0) AS minutes
  FROM ops.job_events AS job_events
  WHERE
    job_events.dt BETWEEN '2026-09-22' AND '2026-09-24'
  GROUP BY
    job_events.job_id,
    job_events.dt
)
INSERT OVERWRITE TABLE mart.job_day_facts PARTITION(dt)
SELECT
  events_per_job.job_id,
  job_owners.team,
  events_per_job.events,
  events_per_job.runs,
  events_per_job.minutes,
  events_per_job.dt
FROM events_per_job
LEFT JOIN ops.job_owners AS job_owners
  ON job_owners.job_id = events_per_job.job_id
  AND job_owners.dt = events_per_job.dt
  AND job_owners.dt BETWEEN '2026-09-22' AND '2026-09-24'
```

Compare the two Markdown files

Python's difflib.ndiff compares two lists of lines and marks each line that only the first holds with "- ", and each that only the second holds with "+ ". changed_lines prints those lines, each under the part of the Markdown file it is in: the Statement, from its ## heading, then the column or the Hive, from the heading under that. It leaves out the last line of each file, which says when the file was made, and so differs every time:

def changed_lines(before_file: str, after_file: str) -> None:
    before = Path(before_file).read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()
    after = Path(after_file).read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()
    part = heading = shown = None
    for line in difflib.ndiff(before, after):
        text = line[2:]
        if text.startswith("## "):
            part, heading = text[3:], None
        elif text.startswith("###"):
            heading = text.lstrip("# ")
        if line.startswith(("- ", "+ ")) and not text.startswith("Made by export_lineage"):
            where = part if heading is None else f"{part}, {heading}"
            if where != shown:
                print(f"In {where}:")
                shown = where
            print(line[:100])
changed_lines("before.md", "after.md")

Common mistakes

Exporting the Statements built before the change

A Statement holds its Building block as it was when it was built. Change the file, but export the Statements you already had, and the Lineage after looks just like the one before. Here team_day_before was built before the change, and still counts a failed run's minutes:

"IN ('finish', 'fail')" in to_hive(team_day_before)

Python shows

True
"IN ('finish', 'fail')" in to_hive(team_day)

Python shows

False

Build the Statements again after each change, with build_statements, then export. A function you imported yourself from the Building block also stays as it was until you restart the notebook's kernel: project.load reads the files again each time, an import of your own doesn't.

Comparing two DataFrames with ==

== between two DataFrames compares them cell by cell and gives back a third DataFrame, of True and False. assert can't say whether a whole DataFrame is true, so it stops:

facts_write, team_day = build_statements("2026-09-18")
result = run_query(team_day, query)
expected = oracle(rows_of("2026-09-18"), ending=["finish"])
assert result == expected

Python stops with this message

ValueError:
The truth value of a DataFrame is ambiguous. Use a.empty, a.bool(), a.item(), a.any() or a.all().

Compare lists of rows, as same_rows does, or use pandas' own pd.testing.assert_frame_equal.

Comparing rows in the order they came back

The Example database gives rows in a fixed order, but your warehouse gives them in no fixed order. Compare without sorting, and a right answer fails whenever the order differs, as it does here, with the most minutes first:

most_first = expected.sort_values("minutes", ascending=False)
result.to_dict("records") == most_first.to_dict("records")

Python shows

False
same_rows(result, most_first)

Python shows

True

Put both in one order before comparing, as same_rows does with "team".

An oracle that asks the Statement

An oracle built from the Statement's own result always agrees with it, right or wrong. No message stops you:

same_rows(result, result)

Python shows

True

Work the oracle out from the rows themselves, as oracle does from rows_of, and in another way than the Statement does.

20. Choose how a Saved table is stored Intermediate

Goal

Say in a Saved table's Table reference how the warehouse keeps it: the folder of its own its files go in, whether dropping it deletes them, their format, its Partitions, and Buckets. create_table writes all of it, and check_table_reference compares it with the table. Along the way, see why the Toolbox has no indexes, and what makes reads fast instead.

When you'd use it

When you fill in a Saved table's Table reference, and when you check one you already have: every Saved table needs at least its folder. The rest is for when a table grows: a big table read a region at a time, or joined on the same column every run, can be kept so that reads touch fewer files.

It needs Save a table, which makes a Saved table with project.new_table.

Steps

Start from the Intermediate Example project

Work in a copy of the Intermediate Example project, at its top: copy example_projects/intermediate/ from the download to a folder of your own, copy the sqlglot_composer folder into it, as a Project holds it, and open a notebook there. This page makes the same copy in its first step, from the download the Toolbox came in, into the folder it runs in, which Python's path holds already, as Jupyter's does for a notebook's own folder:

import shutil
from pathlib import Path
import sqlglot_composer
download = Path(sqlglot_composer.__file__).parents[1]  # -> Path
_ = shutil.copytree(download / "example_projects" / "intermediate", ".", dirs_exist_ok=True)

"""mart - a Database: written by the Project actions, never by hand.

Why: `from references import mart` gives each of its Table references by its name, so a column
is reached as mart.budget_overruns.job_id.

job_events_checks (references/mart__job_events_checks.py), job_notes
(references/mart__job_notes.py), job_region_costs (references/mart__job_region_costs.py),
team_days (references/mart__team_days.py), team_failures (references/mart__team_failures.py).

The Project actions and refresh_reference_sheet write this file again from the Table
references in references/, so a change made here is lost. A Table reference with a <...> still
in it, as new_table writes one, is left out until it is filled in.
"""

import difflib
from typing import NoReturn

from references.mart__budget_overruns import budget_overruns
from references.mart__job_day_costs import job_day_costs
from references.mart__job_day_facts import job_day_facts
from references.mart__job_events_checks import job_events_checks
from references.mart__job_notes import job_notes
from references.mart__job_region_costs import job_region_costs
from references.mart__team_days import team_days
from references.mart__team_failures import team_failures

# Its tables, by the names tab completion lists and a wrong name's message gives: the names
# `from references.mart import *` gives, too.
__all__ = ["budget_overruns", "job_day_costs", "job_day_facts", "job_events_checks", "job_notes", "job_region_costs", "team_days", "team_failures"]
_TABLES = __all__


def __getattr__(name: str) -> NoReturn:
    """A name that isn't one of its tables: say which tables it has, and the closest."""
    if name.startswith("_"):
        raise AttributeError(name)
    close = difflib.get_close_matches(name, _TABLES, n=1)
    hint = f" Did you mean {close[0]!r}?" if close else ""
    raise AttributeError(f"mart has no table {name!r}.{hint} Its tables are: "
                         f"{', '.join(_TABLES)}.", obj=None)


def __dir__() -> list[str]:
    """Its tables, so tab completion lists them."""
    return list(_TABLES)

from references import mart, ops
job_region_costs, region_costs = mart.job_region_costs, ops.region_costs  # -> Table, Table
Give it a folder of its own

Every Saved table is an external table: its files are yours, in a folder you name. You give location= the table's own folder, and the Toolbox writes it exactly as you give it, adding nothing. A folder named after the database and the table, such as /data/your_team/mart.db/job_region_costs, keeps each table's folder apart.

A folder of its own matters because the warehouse reads every file in a table's folder. Two tables in one folder read each other's rows, and an INSERT OVERWRITE of a Partition in one can delete the other's files for that Partition. The Toolbox refuses a Table reference whose folder is another Saved table's, or sits inside it.

A path you would rather not write out in every Table reference can start with a Hive variable, such as location="${hivevar:root}/mart.db/job_region_costs": the Toolbox writes it as it is, and Hive fills it in from a SET hivevar:root=/data/your_team sent first, with hive_settings(..., sets=...) as Keep reads and joins fast sends its settings.

Say what dropping it does

purge=True makes dropping the table delete its files too. Left out, or purge=False, the warehouse only forgets the table: its files stay in its folder, and a table created there again gets the old rows back once repair_partitions lists their Partitions. Keep purge=True for a table you rebuild from its sources; leave it out for one whose files you would want back.

Choose its file format

stored_as= is the file format: "ORC", the usual one and what you get when you leave it out, which Hive reads fastest, or "PARQUET", which more tools outside Hive read. compression= is how its files are packed: ORC's "ZLIB" makes smaller files, "SNAPPY" faster ones. properties= takes any other table property. create_table writes them all:

text = show_hive(create_table(job_region_costs, may_exist=True))  # -> str

Hive, ready to paste

CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE IF NOT EXISTS mart.job_region_costs (
  job_id BIGINT,
  cost_cents BIGINT,
  PRIMARY KEY (job_id, region, dt) DISABLE NOVALIDATE
)
PARTITIONED BY (
  region STRING,
  dt STRING
)
STORED AS ORC
LOCATION '/data/your_team/mart.db/job_region_costs'
TBLPROPERTIES (
  'external.table.purge'='true',
  'orc.compress'='ZLIB',
  'made_by'='mart__job_region_costs.ipynb'
);
Choose its Partitions

partitioned_by=["region", "dt"] keeps each region's rows in a folder of their own, and each of its days in a folder inside that, as ops.region_costs does. A Statement that filters region reads only that region's folders, and one that filters dt too reads fewer still. A table's Partitions are whichever columns its reads filter most: a region, a day, a load, or none at all, as the Example project's mart.job_notes has none.

A write fills each Partition from its rows' own values, so its SELECT names every partition column, anywhere: the Toolbox puts them last, in the order partitioned_by= gives, where Hive reads them from. Here ops.region_costs writes its days like 20260924, and mart.job_region_costs keeps them that way, since the Toolbox writes each value exactly as it is given:

def write_days(first_day: str, last_day: str) -> Statement:
    return statement(
        INSERT_OVERWRITE(job_region_costs),
        SELECT(region_costs.job_id, region_costs.region, region_costs.dt,
               AS(sum_of(region_costs.cost_cents), "cost_cents")),
        FROM(region_costs),
        WHERE(between(region_costs.dt, first_day, last_day)),
        GROUP_BY(region_costs.job_id, region_costs.region, region_costs.dt),
    )
text = show_hive(write_days("20260922", "20260924"))

Hive, ready to paste

-- The Session setting "dynamic_partitions": this write fills region, dt from its rows.
SET hive.exec.dynamic.partition=true;
SET hive.exec.dynamic.partition.mode=nonstrict;
INSERT OVERWRITE TABLE mart.job_region_costs PARTITION(region, dt)
SELECT
  region_costs.job_id,
  SUM(region_costs.cost_cents) AS cost_cents,
  region_costs.region,
  region_costs.dt
FROM ops.region_costs AS region_costs
WHERE
  region_costs.dt BETWEEN '20260922' AND '20260924'
GROUP BY
  region_costs.job_id,
  region_costs.region,
  region_costs.dt;

The columns in PARTITION(...) have no value: the warehouse takes each row's region and dt from the SELECT's last columns. Doing so is Hive's dynamic partitioning, which a Session setting switches on, so show_hive prints its two SET lines first. run_execute sends the write alone: send the Session setting first, with hive_settings, before the first such write. The warehouse keeps it for as long as your execute's connection lasts, and sending it again does no harm. project.run_tables() sends it for you. Here it goes to the Example database's execute, which prints each SET line:

run_execute(hive_settings("dynamic_partitions"), execute)

Python prints

execute: SET hive.exec.dynamic.partition=true
execute: SET hive.exec.dynamic.partition.mode=nonstrict

INSERT OVERWRITE replaces only the Partitions its rows hold: a region and day with no rows keeps whatever it held before. So if a region drops out of the table you read, its old rows stay in the Saved table until you drop them with the admin module's drop_partitions.

A write can name some Partitions itself instead, with partition={...}: here the eu region, whose rows then leave region out of SELECT. The columns it names come first in partitioned_by=, and the rest are filled from the rows:

text = show_hive(statement(
    INSERT_OVERWRITE(job_region_costs, partition={"region": "eu"}),
    SELECT(region_costs.job_id, region_costs.dt,
           AS(sum_of(region_costs.cost_cents), "cost_cents")),
    FROM(region_costs),
    WHERE(equals(region_costs.region, "eu"),
          between(region_costs.dt, "20260922", "20260924")),
    GROUP_BY(region_costs.job_id, region_costs.dt),
))

Hive, ready to paste

-- The Session setting "dynamic_partitions": this write fills dt from its rows.
SET hive.exec.dynamic.partition=true;
SET hive.exec.dynamic.partition.mode=nonstrict;
INSERT OVERWRITE TABLE mart.job_region_costs PARTITION(region = 'eu', dt)
SELECT
  region_costs.job_id,
  SUM(region_costs.cost_cents) AS cost_cents,
  region_costs.dt
FROM ops.region_costs AS region_costs
WHERE
  region_costs.region = 'eu' AND region_costs.dt BETWEEN '20260922' AND '20260924'
GROUP BY
  region_costs.job_id,
  region_costs.dt;
Add Buckets only to a big table

bucketed_by= with buckets= spreads each Partition's rows into that many files by the values of some columns, and sorted_by= sorts the rows in each. A join on those columns can then pair file with file instead of reading everything. It pays off only on big tables, tens of millions of rows a Partition, joined on those columns; and changing it means writing the whole table again. Most Saved tables need none. Say mart.event_facts, every event with its minutes, is such a table, joined on job_id every run:

project.new_table("mart.event_facts")

Hive

CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE mart.event_facts (
  event_id BIGINT,
  job_id BIGINT,
  minutes INT,
  PRIMARY KEY (event_id) DISABLE NOVALIDATE
)
PARTITIONED BY (
  dt STRING
)
CLUSTERED BY (job_id) SORTED BY (job_id) INTO 16 BUCKETS
STORED AS ORC
LOCATION '/data/your_team/mart.db/event_facts'
Why there are no indexes

Hive removed indexes in its version 3, so the Toolbox writes none. What makes a read fast instead:

  • Partitions: a Statement that filters a partition column, as every Load limit insists, opens only those Partitions' folders, and one that filters a second partition column too opens fewer still.
  • Fewer, larger files: ORC and Parquet files keep each column's smallest and largest values, so the warehouse skips the parts of a file a condition rules out, and a few large files open faster than many small ones.
  • Buckets, for big tables joined on the same columns, as above.
  • Statistics: once the warehouse has counted a table's rows and values, it picks how to join it, such as sending a small table to every machine instead of sorting both.

Keep reads and joins fast shows the last three at work.

A folder that isn't a table's own may hold other tables' files: two tables in one folder read each other's files, and an INSERT OVERWRITE of a Partition in one can delete the other's files for that Partition.
